featured.title: 20 Trends for Good UI in 2020
featured.subtitle: DARIA GORODNIA, MBA, PSPO on LinkedIn

slides.title: 20 Trends for Good UI in 2020
slides.subtitle: DARIA GORODNIA, MBA, PSPO on LinkedIn
slides.description: The vast importance of good User Interface (UI) design has become a universal truth. Start-ups and large household brands alike invest in the visual and experiential appeal of their digital touch points. With UI being at intersection of aesthetic and function as a discipline, there are limitless possible designs that can be created. But, as a case with fashion, several trends are shaping many of today’s digital brand assets, with common application across websites, eCommerce platforms, and marketing. While trends are not exhaustive and should not limit one’s creativity, they can be directional and inspiring when modernizing current or designing new digital assets. Here goes the list of my top 20 trends in UI, in no particular order for now, and later organized by focus area. 1. Storytelling 2. Editorial photography 3. Asymmetry & split screen 4. Brazen bold typography (and other creative fonts) 5. Illustrations & animations 6. Broken grid 7. Bright & monochrome colors 8. Empty space & minimalism 9. Overlapping typography 10. Dark theme 11. Gradients & liquid gradients 12. Custom navigation 13. Blended experiences 14. Long & parallax scrolling 15. Full screen visuals 16. Visual eCommerce & frameless design 17. Uninterrupted UX 18. Data visualization 19. Gesture navigation 20. Micro interactions Now, let’s look beyond the list and see how these trends are applied to digital assets to elevate “look and feel” and user experience of brands across industries. But first, let’s bucket them into logical categories for an easier discussion: Storytelling, Layout, Navigation, Visual Elements, and Graphic Design. But before we jump in, a couple words of caution must be said. First, none of the listed trends should be viewed in vacuum. Indeed, many of the examples below illustrate multiple trends being used concurrently. Second, while trends can give inspiration for modernizing your digital assets, they should never supersede your core brand identity. Okay, now, let’s dive in. I. Trends in Storytelling Storytelling is the “How of UI”. It is an overarching art that blends visual elements and narrative to tell a story and showcase products in a progressive intuitive way by using meaningful content, sequential story & visual integration, and human tone. Storytelling is so important that it’s a category in itself. In fact, if you were to adapt only one of these trends, storytelling would have to be the one. The other trends can help bring your story to life, but you would first need a strong story to tell. Let’s look at a couple of examples of storytelling done right. Thrillist Magazine brings its story to life by blending multimedia content, including visuals, articles, and even music. UDX Bike transforms a traditional product-oriented website into a narrative with sequential visuals and value proposition messaging. II. Trends in Layout Trends in layout are all about placing page contents in a natural sight path, while breaking out from the conventional approach. Broken grid Grid is used to organize digital elements in a way that makes them easy to digest. While designing for the grid has multiple benefits, it can also make websites look very traditional and similar-looking. That is why breaking out from the grid without sacrificing content digestibility can be an effective way to make your site stand out and engage users in a more unexpected way. Stories + Objects uses broken grid to feature stories and objects in an unconventional format. Split screen Split screen is another form of unconventional layout. It places various forms of content side-by-side in a way that is both symmetrical from the content ratio and asymmetrical from the content type perspective. Bose uses a form of split screen to feature its new products and bring pictures and specs front and center while engaging users with unique UI and navigation. Blended experiences & overlapping typography With all the different types of content that exist today, blending them together is one sure way to get noticed and bring focus to several visuals at the same time. While blending content types can be very effective, it can also be overwhelming for users to digest, if not done right. So be careful with this one. Here, Allpress uses blended experiences with video and image content alongside overlapping typography to create dynamism in its website. Empty space & minimalism Almost a polar opposite of the previous trend, another way to bring content to focus is to surround it with a lot of empty space. Think simplistic minimalistic design. Tinker Watches applies minimalism and empty space to communicate brand elegance and classic style of its products. III. Trends in Navigation UI trends in navigation are focused on enabling a more fluid, seamless, intuitive and interactive engagement experience. Custom navigation Tired of standard buttons and side bar menus? Custom navigation commands can help engage users but must be used with caution to avoid frustrating them with unfamiliar commends that are not intuitive to use. Steelcase blends imagery and interactive elements to create custom navigation where users can click directly on the visuals to move between different site assets. Uninterrupted UX What if we didn’t have to click “Next” or navigate to site pages manually? That is what uninterrupted UX trend is trying to address by applying visual effects and transitions that connect site pages in a fluid manner, making users feel as if they are always just scrolling the same page. This bike configurator concept for Bikeville makes use of uninterrupted UX with special transition effects to create a fluid experience as users move through the bike configuration process. Long & parallax scrolling Long scrolling has been around for a while but still continues to prove successful in many applications and across devices. It relies on scrolling down the page instead of manually moving from page to page. It works particularly well on mobile devices. Think Instagram, Facebook, other social media and news sites. The parallax effect is also still widely used across websites, particularly in combination with long scrolling page design. Gucci made to best use of long scrolling in its spring-summer collection microsite to immerse users into the story behind the collection and evoke emotional response. Micro interactions It can be frustrating to interact with a website or an app that isn’t visibly responsive to every click or touch. Users need that physical feedback, whether a slight vibration under their fingertips or a visible movement of an icon that signals immediate response. This is what micro interactions are there to address. In the form of icons, buttons and shapes, they create a sense of movement, action and response, making for a more dynamic user experience. Care/Of uses multiple dynamic icons that indicate motion and make the site look more responsive to users. Visual eCommerce & frameless design It’s no news that users respond well to visuals and have even come to expect high quality images and videos across all digital touch points. Indeed, in a survey, 90% of Etsy users said that product image quality impacted their purchase decisions. This notion is driving UI design where visuals are front and center of user interactions, bringing products and content to life. Joseph leverages impactful visuals with frameless design to enable a more immersive product browsing. Gesture navigation Mobile-first is no longer a trend, but a reality. There are various mobile UI trends that look promising and gesture navigation is one of them. It addresses designing for a different kind of interaction that is native to smaller screen surfaces and fingers of various sizes. Traditional desktop version buttons may not be the best solution when it comes to handheld devices and this is what this trend is aiming to address. This concept example features buttonless gesture navigation to deliver a fully optimized mobile interaction. IV. Trends in Visual Elements Visual elements could be content, functional or interactive components of a digital touchpoint. The following trends are all about making the best use of visual elements to enrich user experience. Editorial photography While pictures are widely used across digital touch points, some brands are taking product photography to the next level. Two styles are gaining popularity – “micro” “close up” “hero” shots and lifestyle photography where products are featured as part of everyday routines. The quality bar is also raised for both styles – professional production, staging, and editing all play a big role in the end product. Nike, as many fashion brands, posts high quality editorial style photography that features products in a lifestyle setting promoted by the brand. Full screen visuals Another trend that helps maximize the impact of visuals is blowing them up full screen. It is an effective way to grab user attention to tell a story with either editorial photography or impactful video. Another fashion brand, Uterque, makes full use of editorial video content to immerse users into the brand experience and communicate its unique point of view on personal style. Illustrations & animations With brands trying to stand out and own their digital identity, custom illustrations and animations are becoming popular. With those, websites and apps are also becoming more artistic and unique. Lava includes custom illustrations on its website, in line with its brand identity and personality. Data visualization This trend has become a universal truth but still is not applied to its full potential. Data, especially heavy and cumbersome, can be difficult to digest if presented in its raw form. This is where maps, graphs, charts, infographics and other forms of visualization come into play to make data more digestible and impactful for users. The New Yorker used a visualization technic to showcase Citi bike usage pattern on a dynamic map. V. Trends in Graphic Design Colors, fonts, and themes are all ways to impact user perceptions on a sensory level. They can also be used to differentiate brands and emphasize certain content and messaging in digital touch points. Bright & monochrome color palettes Polar opposites of each other, both bold and neutral color palettes are trending. With such variety, it becomes a matter of branding. Splashing colors or pastels – what suits your brand’s personality more? Broken English Taco Pub, a Chicago restaurant chain, uses a lot of bright colors to extend its brand personality across its digital assets. Shinola, a Detroit-based accessory and lifestyle brand, uses pastels and minimalist design to communicate its classy high-end brand image. Bold & creative typography Typography is also trending on the bold side. Large creative fonts with various effects and treatments help make the content and messaging pop. Moschino amplifies its bold branding with bold colors and typography. Gradients & liquid gradients Colors can go a long way and gradients open even more ways to do so. Cotton candy skies and turquoise waters don’t come in one color. Gradients allow more of those unique color palettes into brands’ digital identity. Apple uses gradients in a lot of its designs which have become brand staples. Dark theme Dark colors have always been a staple for classic tasteful elegance. If this style is in line with your brand identity, dark theme may be a good choice for your digital touch points. Apple also extensively leverages dark theme to add sleekness to its products and brand. In conclusion, here are some final thoughts on good UI and how the discussed trends can help to get there. Good UI is: 1. Having a strong story to tell 2. Thinking outside a traditional layout 3. Blending different design elements and themes 4. Designing for interaction 5. Enabling intuitive navigation 6. Utilizing custom and artistic visuals 7. Combining storytelling, graphic elements and visuals in a seamless experience 8. Appealing to natural curiosity and a sense of discovery 9. Anticipating and promoting action 10. Having courage to be different 11. Expressing a unique but consistent aesthetic 12. Evoking an emotional response 13. Staying true to your brand identity __________________ Written by Daria Gorodnia

slides.title: Should Brands Get Political?
slides.subtitle: DARIA GORODNIA, MBA, PSPO on LinkedIn
slides.description: We drink Starbucks to express social status or lifestyle. But at times, some of us drink it or don’t drink it, to express political affiliation. Politics are everywhere – on TV, online, on Facebook, in our conversations, and on our minds. Keeping their fingers on the pulse of the American society and trying to make it into trending discussions, brands start to get political by taking stands on social issues, and by doing so, send politically-charged messages to consumers around the world. Over several recent elections, Starbucks made an announcement supporting refugee employment, Airbnb launched a program on diversity and inclusion, 84 Lumber sent a mixed message on immigration, and Audi took a stand on equal pay for women. While such statements can appeal to thousands of consumers on an emotional level and help brands cut through the clutter by staying relevant in pop culture, they can also be double-edge swords when it comes to impact on brand equity and business performance. So, before taking a side and making a loud statement, brands must evaluate potential gains and risks, make a plan to address business objectives, and prepare to deal with the inevitable backlash from segments of the public. In the evaluation process, the following questions should be considered. Who is the brand’s audience? Many international brands serve hundreds of thousands of consumers on a daily basis. While they need to understand all of their main target segments, they must truly know their best customers. They are brands' most loyal and engaged users who drive product adoption and conversation. By taking a stand on a political issue, brands will inevitably alienate some customers, but they have to be very careful to not alienate the best ones. This is where a deeper look into brand identity and the initial audience is needed. What are the best customers’ sentiments towards a certain political issue? If they are in line with brand sentiments and identity, it may be worth it to speak out. What is the brand’s identity and image? It is critical to ensure that any politically-charged statements issued by a brand are in line with its brand identity, image, and long-term strategy. Neil Golden, former Chief Marketing Officer at McDonalds USA and current Adjunct Lecturer at Northwestern University, says that brands have to be very careful with taking sides on political topics. If a brand has not been historically vocal on the issue, speaking out about it during the time of political unrest and resistance movements may be seen as opportunistic and produce even more backlash from the public. For example, when Starbucks made a statement on refugee employment in 2017, many consumers felt it was a stretch for the brand’s identity. Although Starbucks often speaks for fair employment practices, it hasn’t focused specifically on refugees before. So by making such a loud statement through a press release, Starbucks actually appeared somewhat insincere and opportunistic. Is there a plan in place? Next, it is important to consider any statement as a part of a larger, comprehensive, integrated plan. Airbnb and Audi both took stands on social issues in their 2017 Super Bowl ads. Airbnb ran a #WeAccept spot that stood for diversity and inclusion while Audi ran a highly emotional spot on equal pay for women. Both spots were produced beautifully and evoked feelings and emotional connections with the respective brands. However, from the larger brand communications plan perspective, Airbnb’s statement was better thought out compared to Audi’s. Airbnb reached far above making an emotional connection with the public and into solving an actual business problem with a comprehensive plan. In particular, guest discrimination by hosts was the issue that Airbnb aimed to address, but the timing of a statement on diversity and inclusion could not have been better from the political conversation stand point at that point. Minutes after the Super Bowl ad aired, Airbnb followed up with e-mails to the Airbnb community, both hosts, and guests, asking to accept the brand’s stand. In contrast, it is not clear where Audi’s message fit. The brand did not seem to have any program or plan in place to walk the talk on its advertised commitment to equal pay for women. Interestingly, its well-intentioned message produced backlash from some women who pointed out the lack of diversity in the brand’s leadership ranks. What are the business objectives? Any brand communication should be tied to a business objective. Is the company trying to improve brand awareness or brand image? Is it trying to attract qualified employees? Or perhaps grow sales and acquire new customers? Objectives can be very diverse and span across a variety of business aspects, but at least one has to be addressed by the message. The 2017 Super Bowl spot by 84 Lumber, a brand that then operated only a few locations, puzzled many consumers with a very emotional but rather unclear message on immigration; it wasn’t clear whether the brand supported or opposed it. But most importantly, it was not clear what business objective the brand was trying to solve with a roughly $15M 90-second spot during the most-watched national sporting event. The brand claimed that it aimed to attract a younger employee base, but still, what message did it really send to the rest of the country? All in all, brands are people. They are operated by people, for people. And people have sentiments, opinions, and passions. Politics touch on many emotional strings, making people feel the need to express their stand publicly, to feel support and inclusion. Household brands are often viewed as integral part of consumer lives. Indeed, many consumers view brands as extensions of themselves. As brands become vehicles for self-expression, consumers start to expect them to take a stand and participate in social movements. This expectation gives a new meaning to the social responsibility concept, but brands must not forget to evaluate the aforementioned business considerations. Likewise, it is essential that they stay true to their brand promises when speaking out. This post was originally published in Vitamin IMC, Northwestern University's student blog channel, on February 16, 2017. It has been revised to stay relevant today and provoke thought on brands in politics in the future.

Clients I serve range from large multinationals to small domestic companies.

headline: Senior Designer, Assistant Manager - EY Learning Lab
about:
Currently, I serve as an advisory consultant with expertise in design and learning services. Over the course of my career, I have been both a collaborative team member and creative lead on innovative, problem-solving teams. I am results-driven and am able to complete multiple, complex projects on time and within budget in a fast-paced environment. 

For over ten years, my focus has been on designing custom digital training solutions with an emphasis on elegant user interface design, accessible user experiences, and mobile-first design. I hold a degree in Art Direction, including an understanding of front-end coding and the limitations surrounding digital platforms. 

I find joy in the creative process every step of the way from concept ideation, to creating mockups and prototypes, to the final client presentation. Some of my strongest work has been in learning strategy, brand adherence, identity design, interactive PDFs, and custom asset/animation creation and management. I have worked with clients in the Airline, Banking & Capital Markets, Government, Utilities, Food & Beverage, Information Technology, Medical/Pharmaceutical, Real Estate, Social Justice, Higher Ed, Hospitality, and Retail industries. While my focus is digital, I am also well-versed in print collateral design such as pamphlets, booklets, invitations, posters, and other marketing materials. 

I approach my work holistically with central values such as kindness, empathy, and inclusion at the core of my leadership style. It's my belief that a positive collaborative working experience starts with open and honest conversation and a willingness to try new ideas. I am an active member of my community through several volunteer roles and stay creative as an independent artist. I am the owner and artist of Lunaria Creative Goods on Etsy.

headline: Senior Manager @ EY | Leading Workday-Enabled Finance Transformation for Financial Services | Workday Financials, Prism, Accounting Center Architecture
about:
Seasoned Workday Finance Architect and EY Senior Manager laser-focused on driving strategic finance transformation within the Financial Services Industry (FSI). With over a decade of experience and 10+ Workday certifications, I partner with Banking, Capital Markets, and Insurance leaders to architect and implement innovative solutions that deliver measurable business value.

My expertise lies in leveraging the full power of Workday Financials – including advanced modules like Workday Prism Analytics, Accounting Center, and Adaptive Planning – to tackle complex FSI challenges. I specialize in designing scalable architectures that optimize core financial processes (R2R, P2P, C2C), streamline consolidations, enhance regulatory reporting (e.g., leveraging Accounting Center for complex subledger requirements), and provide actionable insights through robust analytics (via Prism).

Key areas of impact include:

Architecting enterprise-scale Workday Financials solutions for global FSI organizations.

Leading programs delivering significant operational improvements, such as reducing financial close cycles by up to 50%.

Designing and implementing sophisticated Workday Accounting Center solutions to address intricate FSI accounting standards and subledger integrations.

Leveraging Workday Prism Analytics to build powerful reporting and analytics capabilities, unlocking critical financial and operational insights.

Integrating Workday Financials seamlessly within complex enterprise ecosystems, considering full-platform implications (HCM/Payroll).

Serving as a trusted advisor to C-level executives, translating business strategy into actionable Workday roadmaps.

Prior leadership roles at Alight Solutions (Director) and IBM (Lead Consultant) honed my ability to lead high-performing teams, manage complex stakeholder environments, and deliver tangible results. I am passionate about using technology as a catalyst for change, empowering FSI organizations to achieve greater efficiency, transparency, and strategic agility through Workday.

headline: Associate Director at EY
about:
As an award-winning UX Director with over 15 years of experience in leading-edge design, user experience, and creative direction, I have developed a passion for pushing the boundaries of what is possible in the world of design. I have a proven track record of leading international design teams and exceeding business objectives through my innovative approach to development and creative direction.

My expertise in UX design has been honed through a diverse range of roles, including Creative Director at Connect Healthcare, VP of UX at Doctor.com, and the Lead UX strategist at EY. In each of these positions, I have been responsible for delivering exceptional user experiences across a range of products and services.

Throughout my career, my work has been recognized with numerous awards including multiple eHealthcare leadership awards, Top 40 Account Based Marketing Superhero, and finalist for Computing Technology Innovator of the Year 2022.

My dedication to pushing the boundaries of design is rooted in my education, which includes a BFA in Graphic Design, UX management certifications from NN/g and Interaction Design Foundation, and as a Certified Scrum Master.

I am committed to creating engaging and intuitive user experiences that exceed expectations and drive results for my clients. My passion for design and my commitment to excellence continue to inspire those around me, and I remain dedicated to pushing the boundaries of what is possible in the world of design, user experience, artificial intelligence, and innovative ways of working.

experience.description:
Advanced Design at EY is a human-centered design lab that I lead, focused on driving experience-led innovation and digital transformation. Our team is based in Atlanta, Chicago, New York City, and Wroclaw, and we are passionate, disciplined, collaborative, and restless in our pursuit of delivering exceptional experiences.

We work on intelligent and intuitive digital services, tackling the most complex problems worth solving in an authentic and co-creative manner. We draw inspiration from the innovative technologies that shape our day-to-day lives, such as AI and hyperpersonalization.

Our purpose and mission are to reshape the way professional services are experienced in today's business environment. By putting experience first and working closely with clients, we architect ultimate experiences that not only deliver iconic moments but also transform industries.

We differentiate ourselves by being the best in the field, leading with experience to drive innovation and technology. As sensemakers, we design for the senses, giving profound meaning to every experience. We celebrate innovation, experimentation, and the power of ideas, constantly seeking to make a difference.

Collaborate with XD team leads, stakeholders, and others to define and implement rational, effective, and efficient design processes, methods, and best practices. Serve as senior research and design practitioner, leading activities that span product strategy, user research and discovery, data analysis and insights, conceptual design, information architecture and navigation, and high-level user interface design.

Lead design thinking, product strategy, and innovation workshops. Contribute to XD Group planning, strategy, and promotion. Communicate design decisions and rationale with clarity and authority to stakeholders.

As the VP of User Experience, I’m the primary leader of the UX department. My main goal is to lead the UX department in growth and and excellence by promoting collaboration in the department, creating a positive environment, embodying the business/product values and, assisting in the achievement of product goals.

I also conduct research and documents findings, create consumer scenarios, and create strategy documents and content to supply to the UX department personnel as well as collaborating product departments.  I work closely with other product management departments to ensure consumer requirements and needs are considered and incorporated in the product from the conceptualization to the realization of the product.

As Senior Creative Director at Doctor.com, I oversee a national team of designers and writers responsible for the UX/UI, branding, and creative needs for the entire company. With the help of my team, incredible amounts of research, preparation, testing, and iteration go into every project at Doctor.com, providing for a sleek, robust, and dynamic user experience.

At Connect Healthcare, I oversee all aspects of our creative presence. This includes all marketing, brand standards, commercials as well as online and printed materials.  While here, my work has won over 10 eHealthcare Leadership Awards for best design.

I built the creative department from the ground up and now manage an extremely talented team of designers, developers and writers.

I also develop and manage our client’s website designs including, compositions, analytics, market research, creative briefs, brand standards, front-end development and project management.

Developed new company-wide coding standards for front-end development that has cut new product implementation time by 80%.

Owner and operator of a graphic design, print production, and web development firm. Specializing in brand identity, websites, music and video production.

Clients include: Fuller Hot Rods, Southern Star Tattoo, Inner Mountain Outfitters, The Atlanta Beat, DocAuto and the American Lung Association.

I started off my design career as an intern at Miller Zell and continued to do contract work for them throughout college. I was responsible for presentations, retail design, signage and print collateral.

publications.title: Multimodal release of transforming growth factor-β1 and the BB isoform of platelet derived growth factor from PEGylated fibrin gels
publications.publishedAt: Journal of Controlled Release, Elsevier · Oct 15, 2010
publications.description: We designed a growth factor release system to potentially stabilize neovascularization in the treatment of ischemic tissue. In this study, the release of PDGF-BB and TGF-β1 was controlled with distinct kinetics from injectable PEGylated fibrin gels. Growth factors can be loaded into PEGylated fibrin gels via 3 mechanisms: entrapment, conjugation through a homobifunctional amine reactive PEG linker, and physical affinity with the fibrin matrix. PDGF-BB was entrapped during thrombin-mediated crosslinking leading to a diffusion-controlled release over 2 days. TGF-β1 was both conjugated through the PEG linker and bound to the matrix via physical affinity, delaying the release rate of TGF-β1 up to 10 days. Further, the release rate was highly correlated to gel degradation rate indicating that TGF-β1 release is degradation-controlled. Therefore, by modulating the molar ratio of PEG to fibrinogen, we were able to control the release rate of TGF-β1 without altering the release kinetics of PDGF-BB. The bioactivity of loaded TGF-β1 was maintained upon release as evidenced by the inhibition of cell proliferation. This system could be expanded to incorporate growth factors loaded via 3 schemes with differing release rates from an injectable system allowing for a high degree of flexibility in other combinational drug delivery and tissue engineering systems.

The OneGoal course – as featured in Paul Tough’s bestselling book How Children Succeed – is grounded in a 1400-page curriculum that focuses on developing non-cognitive skills, improving academic performance in core high school classes and standardized tests, enrolling in a match college, and succeeding during the critical first year of college. publications.title: What Is the Future of Actuarial In Insurance?
publications.description:
The insurance industry, like many, is rapidly evolving and innovating in response to persistent growth challenges and key global megatrends like low interest rates, technology innovation customer and distributor expectations and demographics. The challenges and changes facing insurers, while difficult, are also opportunities for transformative change. Agile companies with a strategic focus can emerge as industry leaders, stronger than ever.

The financial management community at insurers (broadly including finance, risk, actuarial and investments) are facing increased pressure to successfully navigate change and drive growth while lowering costs. The need for these teams to work closely together has never been greater.

This paper outlines how actuarial leaders can set a bold vision and help drive transformational change to thrive in a period of unprecedented challenges and opportunities for the industry.

publications.title: Variable Annuity Hedging Survey: Sophistication Gains, Challenges Remain
publications.description:
Hedging programs remain a variable annuity (VA) writer’s primary line of defense against market exposures embedded in ensured benefits. Our latest VA Hedging Strategy survey revealed some clear shifts in the ways these programs are being managed. But have these changes been evolutionary or revolutionary? How are companies dealing with issues such as:
•	Model sophistication, including the use of stochastic interest rate models, volatility surfaces or skew assumptions, and advanced IT infrastructures?
•	Increasingly arduous operational demands?
•	Conflicting results under multiple regulatory and accounting regimes?
Our latest Insights article covers these issues and more. Read the full article here.
